concept: laysa is defective: no imperfective, person/number only

concept: a judgemental qalb-verb sentence has three nominals; the agent is not one of the complements
prompt: A learner analyzes حَسِبَ الطَّالِبُ الدَّرْسَ سَهْلًا ('the student supposed the lesson [was] easy') and marks الطَّالِبُ (the agent, who does the supposing) as a THIRD accusative complement instead of the nominative fa'il. Explain why the agent is not part of the absorbed predication.
expected_answer: A judgemental qalb-verb sentence has THREE nominals: the agent (who thinks/supposes -- nominative, the fa'il) and its two accusative complements (the absorbed predication). الطَّالِبُ is the agent -- the one doing the supposing -- and is not part of the accusative predication; it stays nominative. The corrected reading is حَسِبَ الطَّالِبُ الدَّرْسَ سَهْلًا, with the agent nominative and the two others accusative.
accepted_variants: count three nominals for a judgemental qalb-verb: the nominative agent plus two accusative complements; the agent is not one of the accusatives
the agent who does the supposing stays nominative and is separate from the two absorbed accusative complements
forbidden_answers: the agent of hasiba is a third accusative complement
the accusative agent is correct for hasiba
required_reasoning: three nominals counted for the judgemental qalb-verb frame
the agent identified as nominative and assigned before the complements

concept: each stacked abrogator governs only its own pair
prompt: A learner sees two governors in one span -- إِنَّ الطَّالِبَ كَانَ مُجْتَهِدًا ('indeed the student was diligent') -- and applies inna's single-family signature (ism accusative / khabar nominative) across the WHOLE span, marking the final word as if it were inna's own khabar and demanding it be nominative. Explain why each governor keeps its own separate scope.
expected_answer: There are two separate governors here: إِنَّ governs its own ism (الطَّالِبَ, accusative) and its own khabar, which is the ENTIRE verbal clause كَانَ الطَّالِبُ مُجْتَهِدًا; inside that clause, كَانَ is its own governor over its own ism (a hidden 'he') and its own khabar (accusative under kana, not under inna). Each governor governs only its own pair; a blanket assignment of one family's signature across the whole span corrupts the elements belonging to the other governor.
accepted_variants: inna and kana are two separate governors, each governing only its own pair; the final word is accusative under kana, not under inna's own khabar rule
resolve each governor's scope separately; a single family's case pattern must not be applied across a span containing more than one governor
forbidden_answers: one governor's case pattern applies across the entire span regardless of how many governors are present
the final word must be nominative because it is inna's khabar
required_reasoning: two separate governors (inna and kana) identified in the span
each governor's scope resolved to its own pair of elements
the blanket single-family assignment rejected
